what_it_does: Cryptographic chips — hardware that performs encryption to protect data — are vulnerable to an attack called a power side-channel: by carefully measuring how much electricity the chip draws moment by moment, an attacker can statistically deduce the secret key, because different key values cause subtly different power consumption patterns. One way to fight this is to inject random electrical glitches (brief spikes or dips in voltage) that mask the real power signature. This paper describes GLiTCH, a framework that strategically adds and removes these glitches by adjusting the physical sizes of logic gates to control when signals arrive, which in turn controls the glitch pattern. The optimization is formulated as a Geometric Programming problem — a specific class of mathematical optimization that can be solved efficiently. The authors apply this to three real cipher designs (AES, CLEFIA, and SM4) and report reduced leakage of key information through power measurements.
